a: King Nebuchadnezzar, to all peoples, nations and languages who live in all the earth: May your peace grow greater!
t: A royal letter, or a king's story?
p: The Old Greek has no greeting; it begins in the king's eighteenth year. The Hebrew Bible numbers this letter 3:31.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), numbered 3:31–33; Theodotion (Swete numbers it Daniel 3:98–100); no Qumran scroll preserves 4:1–3
readings.orig: נבוכדנצר מלכא לכל עממיא אמיא ולשניא
readings.en: King Nebuchadnezzar, to all peoples, nations and languages
readings.plain: King Nebuchadnezzar, to all peoples, nations and languages who live in all the earth: May your peace grow greater!

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 4:1)
readings.orig: Ἔτους ὀκτωκαιδεκάτου τῆς βασιλείας Ναβουχοδονοσὸρ εἶπεν
readings.en: In the eighteenth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar he said
readings.plain: In the eighteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar's reign, he said:

why: The Aramaic text and Theodotion both have the royal greeting, and the greeting is part of the book's pattern of royal letters (4:34-37; 6:25-27). The Old Greek is a freer, shorter retelling in places and adds in others; it cannot be shown to come from a better Aramaic text.
b: The Old Greek of chapters 4-6 differs from the Aramaic by more than any other Old Testament book. Here it has no letter greeting and opens in the first person in 'the eighteenth year' of the king, the year before Jerusalem fell (2 Kings 25:8 gives the nineteenth year). It also adds that the king's sin was laying waste 'the house of the living God' (Swete 4:19), leaves out the scene with the Babylonian experts, and has Daniel show the king the meaning of the dream at the start. The eighteenth year ties the king's pride to the destruction of the temple. Most scholars treat these as changes made when the Greek was translated or revised; some think the Old Greek reflects an earlier edition of the chapter. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles print Theodotion's Greek, as the church did from the third century on.

a: and let seven periods pass over him
p: The Aramaic and Theodotion say 'seven periods'; the Old Greek says 'seven years'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (hepta kairoi, Swete Dat 4:13); 4QDan-d (4Q115) is damaged at this place and its words here are restored by the editors, so it is not cited
readings.en: and seven periods shall pass over him
readings.plain: and let seven periods pass over him

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 4:13)
readings.orig: καὶ ἑπτὰ ἔτη βοσκηθῇ σὺν αὐτοῖς
readings.en: and for seven years let him graze with them
readings.plain: and let seven years pass over him

why: The Aramaic 'iddanin' does not say how long a period was, and Theodotion keeps that openness. The Old Greek's 'years' is an explanation. The Plain English Translation follows the Aramaic.
b: The same word recurs in 4:23, 25 and 32 and in 7:25. In the Old Greek the king spends seven years in the wild; this suited readers who wanted a number. The Aramaic leaves the length open. See the note on this verse.

a: Break with your sins by doing what is right, and with your wrongs by showing mercy to the poor
p: The Aramaic says 'righteousness'; both the Old Greek and Theodotion say 'alms'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008). No scroll preserves 4:27 (4QDan-d, 4Q115, covers 4:8-19 only)
readings.orig: וחטאך בצדקה פרק ועויתך במחן ענין
readings.en: and your sins by righteousness break off, and your iniquities by showing favor to the poor
readings.plain: Break with your sins by doing what is right, and with your wrongs by showing mercy to the poor

readings.w: Theodotion (Swete Dat 4:24)
readings.orig: καὶ τὰς ἁμαρτίας σου ἐν ἐλεημοσύναις λύτρωσαι καὶ τὰς ἀδικίας ἐν οἰκτιρμοῖς πενήτων
readings.en: and redeem your sins with alms and your wrongs with pity for the poor
readings.plain: Buy back your sins with alms and your wrongs with pity for the poor.

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 4:24)
readings.orig: καὶ πάσας τὰς ἀδικίας σου ἐλεημοσύναις λύτρωσαι
readings.en: and redeem all your wrongs with alms
readings.plain: Buy back all your wrongs with alms.

why: The Aramaic word is tsidqah, 'righteousness'. Both Greek versions render it 'alms', as Jewish usage of tsedaqah for charity was already growing, and neither can be shown to come from a different Aramaic text. The Plain English Translation follows the Aramaic and keeps the sense of acts of justice and kindness.
b: The Greek wording was carried into Jerome's Vulgate ('redeem your sins with alms') and became a standard text for the Christian teaching on almsgiving; compare Tobit 12:9 (Tobit is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches). Protestant interpreters usually read the Aramaic as a call to turn from sin to just behavior, shown in care for the poor, not as a payment for sin. See the note on this verse.

a: I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored the one who lives forever
p: The Old Greek has a longer and different thanksgiving to the maker of heaven, earth, seas and rivers.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (Swete Dat 4:31, which follows the Aramaic); no scroll preserves this verse (4QDan-a, 4Q112, has a few words of 4:32-33 only)
readings.orig: ולעליא ברכת ולחי עלמא שבחת והדרת
readings.en: and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored the one who lives forever
readings.plain: I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored the one who lives forever

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 4:34)
readings.orig: τῷ ὑψίστῳ ἀνθομολογοῦμαι καὶ αἰνῶ, τῷ κτίσαντι τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰς θαλάσσας καὶ τοὺς ποταμοὺς
readings.en: I give thanks to the Most High and praise him who made heaven, earth, seas and rivers
readings.plain: I give thanks to the Most High and praise him, who made heaven and earth, the seas and the rivers and everything in them

why: The Aramaic and Theodotion agree, and the Aramaic phrase 'the one who lives forever' matches 6:26. The Old Greek chapter is a different, longer composition here and in its ending.
b: In the Old Greek the king spends seven years in the wild, then turns to prayer (Swete 4:30). The praise that follows adds titles such as 'God of gods and Lord of lords and King of kings' and a vow to serve God from now on. The Old Greek therefore makes the king a more complete convert than the Aramaic does. See the note on whether the king converted.

t: A thousand nobles, or two thousand?
p: The Old Greek says the feast was for two thousand, on the day his palace was dedicated.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (Swete Dat 5:1)
readings.en: for a thousand of his nobles
readings.plain: a thousand of his nobles

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 5:1)
readings.en: he invited two thousand men
readings.plain: two thousand of his nobles

why: The Aramaic and Theodotion agree on a thousand. The Old Greek's 'two thousand' belongs to a freer retelling that also adds the dedication of the palace and a long opening about the king's boasting.
b: The Old Greek of chapter 5 opens: the king 'made a great banquet on the day of the dedication of his palace' and invited two thousand men. It adds that he praised the gods of the nations, cast and carved, and gave no praise to the Most High. It then leaves out Daniel's long speech about Nebuchadnezzar (5:18-22), gives the writing as three Greek verbs, and says at the end that 'Artaxerxes the Mede' took the kingdom (5:31).

a: Now call for Daniel, and he will tell you what it means.
p: Two Qumran scrolls seem to have a longer text here, with a verb 'he will read'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (Swete Dat 5:12)
readings.en: Now let Daniel be called and he will declare the interpretation
readings.plain: Now call for Daniel, and he will tell you what it means.

readings.w: 4QDan-b (4Q113) preserves the verb yqr', 'he will read', which the Masoretic Text lacks. 4QDan-a (4Q112) preserves 'and its interpretation he will declare' (ufshrh yhhwh), but the words before it in that scroll, including the 'he will read' phrase, are restored by the editors and are not cited as a scroll's reading
readings.en: Now let Daniel be called, and he will read the writing and declare its interpretation
readings.plain: Now call for Daniel, and he will read the writing and tell you what it means.

why: The Masoretic Text and Theodotion agree. The longer text could be an expansion that matches the king's request in 5:7 and 5:16, and only one scroll preserves the key word, so the Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text and shows the other reading.
b: The queen's promise in the longer text matches what the king asks of the wise men in 5:7 and of Daniel in 5:16: to read the writing and make known its meaning. The shorter text could have lost a phrase, or the longer one could have added it. Other Qumran differences in chapters 4-7 are mostly spelling (for example 5:21 and 6:26 in 4Q113) or word forms (for example 7:28 in 4Q112).

a: As for you, O king, the Most High God gave the kingdom, greatness, honor and majesty to your father Nebuchadnezzar.
p: The Old Greek has nothing for 5:18-22; these five verses go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (Swete Dat 5:18-22); 4QDan-a (4Q112) preserves part of 5:18-19 and 4QDan-b (4Q113) parts of 5:19-22
readings.orig: אנת מלכא אלהא עלאה מלכותא ורבותא ויקרא והדרה יהב לנבכדנצר אבוך
readings.en: You, O king, the Most High God gave the kingdom, greatness, honor and majesty to Nebuchadnezzar your father
readings.plain: As for you, O king, the Most High God gave the kingdom, greatness, honor and majesty to your father Nebuchadnezzar.

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it): Daniel 5:18-22 are empty and 5:23 follows 5:17
readings.en: (nothing)

why: Two Qumran copies and Theodotion have the recital, which is the center of the chapter's argument (Belshazzar 'knew all this', 5:22). The Old Greek omits it, probably as part of its freer retelling.
b: Without these verses the Old Greek never says why the writing came, beyond the king praising gods of metal and stone and not the God of the ages. The Aramaic chapter has Daniel link the feast to chapter 4 by naming the lesson the king failed to learn (5:21). This is a clear case of how different the Old Greek of chapters 4-6 is. Switching to the second reading removes this verse only; 5:19-22 are missing from the Old Greek as well.

p: Theodotion writes the words once as mane, thekel, phares; the Old Greek translates them as three verbs.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008). No scroll preserves 5:25
readings.en: mene mene teqel ufarsin
readings.plain: Mene, mene, tekel, and parsin

readings.w: Theodotion (Swete Dat 5:25)
readings.en: mane, thekel, phares
readings.plain: Mene, tekel, peres

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 5:17): the Aramaic words are not given; three Greek verbs stand instead
readings.en: numbered, reckoned, taken away
readings.plain: Numbered, reckoned, taken away

why: The Aramaic text has the doubled mene and the plural parsin, which Daniel then reads as the singular peres (5:28). Theodotion shortens it to match his interpretation, and the Old Greek changes both words and meaning.
b: The Old Greek's interpretation says 'the time of your kingship is numbered, your kingdom is coming to an end' (5:26), 'cut short and finished' (5:27), and 'your kingdom is given to the Medes and Persians' (5:28). It is a different tradition of the story. Theodotion's 'mane, thekel, phares' gives each word once, which matches the three interpretations in 5:26-28.

a: Darius the Mede received the kingdom when he was about sixty-two years old.
t: Darius the Mede, or Artaxerxes the Mede?
p: The Old Greek names the Mede 'Artaxerxes' and gives no age. The Hebrew Bible numbers this verse 6:1.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), numbered 6:1; Theodotion (Swete Dat 5:31)
readings.orig: ודריוש מדיא קבל מלכותא כבר שנין שתין ותרתין
readings.en: and Darius the Mede received the kingdom, about sixty-two years old
readings.plain: Darius the Mede received the kingdom when he was about sixty-two years old.

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 5:31)
readings.orig: καὶ Ἀρταξέρξης ὁ τῶν Μήδων παρέλαβε τὴν βασιλείαν
readings.en: And Artaxerxes the Mede took the kingdom
readings.plain: Artaxerxes the Mede received the kingdom.

why: The Aramaic and Theodotion agree on 'Darius', the name used throughout the Aramaic chapters (6:1, 9, 25, 28). The Old Greek's 'Artaxerxes' is probably a different guess at an unfamiliar name.
b: In the Old Greek of chapter 6, Darius is 'full of days and glorious in old age' (6:1). Nothing outside Daniel identifies a Median king under either name. See the note on Darius the Mede.

p: The Old Greek has 127 satraps, the number of provinces in Esther 1:1, and a different plot.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (Swete Dat 6:1); 4QDan-b (4Q113) begins at 6:7 and does not preserve this verse
readings.en: one hundred and twenty satraps
readings.plain: one hundred twenty satraps

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 6:1)
readings.en: one hundred and twenty-seven satraps
readings.plain: one hundred twenty-seven satraps

why: The Aramaic and Theodotion agree on 120. The Old Greek's 127 may have come from Esther 1:1.
b: The Old Greek of chapter 6 differs in more than the number: the overseers are 'three men' set over the satraps, and the plot is the work of two young men (6:4-5), not of the whole body of officials. The ban forbids requests to any god 'except Darius', and Daniel 'falls on his face' (6:10). It ends by saying Darius 'was added to his people' and Cyrus took his kingdom (6:28).

a: Those men said to one another
p: The Old Greek has two young men plan the ban; the Aramaic has all the officials.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (Swete Dat 6:5)
readings.en: Then those men said
readings.plain: Those men said to one another

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 6:4-5)
readings.orig: οἱ δύο νεανίσκοι πρὸς ἀλλήλους λέγοντες
readings.en: the two young men said to each other
readings.plain: The two young men said to each other

why: The Aramaic and Theodotion agree, and the Aramaic reading fits the later scene of a crowd of officials (6:6, 11, 15).
b: In the Old Greek the plot is the work of two men, and the two men thrown to the lions in 6:24 are those two, with their wives and children (Swete 6:24). The whole body of satraps appears only in a smaller role. It is a tighter story than the Aramaic one.

a: So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and during the reign of Cyrus the Persian.
p: Greek Daniel adds a story of Daniel and Cyrus, Bel and the dragon, with Daniel in the lions' den a second time.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008). Bel and the Dragon is not here. In Theodotion's order, as in the Vulgate, it stands at the end of the book as chapter 14; in Papyrus 967, as its editors report, Bel and Susanna follow chapter 12
readings.orig: ודניאל דנה הצלח במלכות דריוש ובמלכות כורש פרסאה
readings.en: And this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian
readings.plain: So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and during the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

readings.w: Greek Daniel (Theodotion and the Old Greek), Bel and the Dragon, given here in summary. It is in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament as 'Daniel 14' and is called one of the Additions to Daniel; it is not in the Hebrew Bible or in Protestant Bibles
readings.orig: Καὶ ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἀστυάγης προσετέθη πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας αὐτοῦ, καὶ παρέλαβεν Κῦρος ὁ Πέρσης τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτοῦ
readings.en: And King Astyages was laid with his fathers, and Cyrus the Persian took his kingdom
readings.plain: Under Cyrus the Persian, Daniel is the king's close friend. The Babylonians worship an idol, Bel, to whom twelve measures of flour, forty sheep and six jars of wine are given each day, and the king says the god eats it. Daniel laughs, has ashes scattered on the temple floor at night, and in the morning shows the king the footprints of the priests, their wives and children, who came in by a secret door. Cyrus has them killed and gives Bel to Daniel to destroy. Then the people worship a great serpent, a dragon. Daniel feeds it cakes of pitch, fat and hair, and it bursts. The people force the king to hand Daniel over, and he is thrown into the lions' den with seven lions, and stays there six days. The prophet Habakkuk, carrying a meal for reapers in Judea, is carried by an angel by his hair to Babylon to feed Daniel. On the seventh day the king finds Daniel alive, praises the God of Daniel, and has his accusers thrown to the lions.

why: The Plain English Translation translates the Hebrew and Aramaic text of Daniel, as the Plain English Translation of Esther does. Bel and the Dragon is in no Hebrew or Aramaic manuscript; Jerome's preface to Daniel lists it among the parts that are not in the Hebrew. The site shows it as a variant and names the work the Additions to Daniel.
b: The story is set under Cyrus, which is why it sits beside chapter 6. It repeats the lions' den (6:16-24) with a new rescue by a prophet. Habakkuk, a prophet of about 600 BC, appears in the time of Cyrus, a historical oddity. The story is an anti-idol tale that matches the Bible's mockery of idols that eat nothing (Isaiah 44:9-20; Jeremiah 10; the Letter of Jeremiah, which is Baruch 6). Catholic and Orthodox churches hold it as Scripture; Protestant churches print it, if at all, among the Apocrypha; Jews do not count it. The Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three, and Susanna, are handled at chapters 3 and 1 of this book.

p: The Aramaic and Theodotion say 'with the clouds'; the Old Greek says 'on the clouds', the preposition of Matthew 26:64.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (Swete Dat 7:13: μετὰ τῶν νεφελῶν). 4QDan-b (4Q113) does not preserve this verse
readings.en: with the clouds of heaven
readings.plain: with the clouds of heaven

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 7:13: ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν)
readings.orig: ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ὡς υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἤρχετο
readings.en: on the clouds of heaven one like a son of man was coming
readings.plain: on the clouds of heaven one like a son of man was coming

why: The Aramaic and Theodotion agree, and 'with' is the ordinary sense of the Aramaic im. The Old Greek's 'on' may be an interpretation that makes the figure ride the clouds, as God does elsewhere in the Old Testament (Psalm 68:4; Isaiah 19:1).
b: Matthew 26:64 has epi ('on') and Mark 14:62 has meta ('with') where Jesus speaks to the high priest, so the two Gospels line up with the two Greek forms of Daniel. Scholars debate whether this shows that either evangelist knew a particular Greek text of Daniel, since epi and meta could each be a natural way to put the picture in Greek. See the note on how the New Testament uses 7:13.

a: He came to the Ancient of Days
t: Came to the Ancient of Days, or appeared as the Ancient of Days?
p: The Old Greek says the one like a son of man was present 'like an ancient of days', not that he came to him.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Theodotion (Swete Dat 7:13: ἕως τοῦ παλαιοῦ τῶν ἡμερῶν ἔφθασεν); 4QDan-b (4Q113) preserves parts of 7:1-6 and 7:11 but not this verse
readings.en: and he reached the Ancient of Days
readings.plain: He came to the Ancient of Days

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 7:13: καὶ ὡς παλαιὸς ἡμερῶν παρῆν). Papyrus 967, the other Old Greek witness, is reported by the editors; its text here was not read for this site
readings.orig: καὶ ὡς παλαιὸς ἡμερῶν παρῆν· καὶ οἱ παρεστηκότες παρῆσαν αὐτῷ
readings.en: and like an ancient of days he was present, and those standing by were present with him
readings.plain: He appeared like the Ancient of Days, and those standing by were with him

why: The Aramaic text and Theodotion agree, and a human figure brought into the court and given a kingdom (7:14) fits 'came to'. Scholars disagree whether the Old Greek reading comes from a different Aramaic text, from a slip in Greek, or from a deliberate rereading.
b: The Old Greek reading would have the son of man share the appearance of the Ancient of Days, or be the same as him. Scholars disagree about its source. Ziegler's Göttingen edition, following Montgomery, treats hos palaios as a corruption of heos tou palaiou ('to the ancient one'); Lust argues that the Old Greek identifies the two figures, and Reynolds (Biblica 89, 2008) that it makes the figure resemble the Ancient of Days and presents him as a messianic figure. These accounts are reported here from the literature, not checked in the editions. Revelation 1:13-14 gives Christ the features of both figures, and a later Jewish debate (Hagigah 14a) shows that 'one throne or two' was already being asked.

a: the people of the holy ones of the Most High
t: A people, or the holy ones themselves?
p: The Aramaic says 'the people of the holy ones'; the Old Greek 'a holy people'; Theodotion has only 'the holy ones'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QDan-a (4Q112) preserves "to the people" (l-am) before the words the editors restore
readings.en: to the people of the holy ones of the Most High
readings.plain: the people of the holy ones of the Most High

readings.w: Old Greek (Codex Chisianus 88, as Swete prints it, Daniel 7:27: λαῷ ἁγίῳ ὑψίστῳ)
readings.en: to a holy people of the Most High
readings.plain: a holy people of the Most High

readings.w: Theodotion (Swete Dat 7:27: ἁγίοις Ὑψίστου)
readings.en: to the holy ones of the Most High
readings.plain: the holy ones of the Most High

why: The Aramaic is supported by the Qumran word 'to the people' and is the harder reading. The Old Greek and Theodotion each simplify it in a different direction.
b: The three readings point to three views of who the holy ones are. 'The people of the holy ones' separates the people from the holy ones (angels, or Israel's martyrs). 'A holy people' is Israel itself. 'The holy ones' alone fits either. The word 'people' also appears in 8:24 and 12:7. See the note at 7:18.
